content.title: About
content.content: Pig in a blanket are bite‑size snacks consisting of small sausages wrapped in flaky or yeasted dough. They are commonly served hot as an appetizer, bar snack, or part of a festive spread. The “1818” version refers to the classic recipe popular in the United States and the United Kingdom.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in the United States in the early 20th century as quick street food.
The name comes from the resemblance of the finished product to a tiny pig wrapped in a “blanket” of dough.
In the UK a similar snack is called a “corn‑wurst” where a sausage is wrapped in a simple flour‑water dough.
There are many dough variations: puff pastry, yeasted dough, wheat‑based, or gluten‑free.
In the US they are often served with mustard, ketchup, or honey‑mustard dipping sauce.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: The sausage provides animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: Combined dough and meat give a quick source of calories useful during high physical activity.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and yeasted dough are rich in B1, B2, and B12 vitamins, supporting nervous system function.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Sausages supply iron, important for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Calcium (when using milk‑based dough)
items.content: Dough made with milk adds calcium, beneficial for bone health.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Sausages often contain a lot of salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Fatty sausage varieties increase saturated fat intake.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional dough contains wheat; people with celiac disease need a gluten‑free version.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Some sausages contain nitrites and other preservatives that should be limited.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pig in a blanket are usually baked in the oven or pan‑fried until golden brown, then served hot with mustard, ketchup, cheese sauce, or honey‑mustard dip. They pair well with fresh vegetables or a simple salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked pieces in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Frozen portions keep for up to 2 months; reheat at 180 °C until crisp. Do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours.
